story.title: AI less regulated than milk, Microsoft president says in warning over safety - The Guardian

facts.text: Artificial intelligence is less regulated than milk and washing machines, the president of Microsoft has said, as the tech industry warns over the safety of AI.
Microsoft, which operates AI infrastructure and is a shareholder in the ChatGPT owner, OpenAI, is led by chief executive Satya Nadella.
On Saturday, Nadella also called for AI models to have an “emergency brake”.
Every carton of milk that you see in the grocery store is subject to safety rules and inspection.”
Microsoft president Brad Smith believes they are not, arguing that everyday products such as milk and washing machines face stricter safety requirements than AI systems.

His warning comes amid concerns over autonomous AI agents, cybersecurity threats and corporate accountability.Why does Microsoft want stricter AI rules?In an interview with the BBC, Smith called for stronger safeguards governing artificial intelligence, including legal accountability when rogue AI agents cause harm.“Right now, your washing machine is subject to more safety rules than AI.

Geoffrey Irving, a former chief scientist at the UK's AI Security Institute, warned about the risk of hostile countries stealing powerful AI models, according to The Guardian.The risks are not limited to cybersecurity.

Brad Smith, Microsoft’s president, has told the BBC that AI is currently working with fewer safety rules than commodities like milk or washing machines, and this should push governments, with the UK out front, to write binding controls, including kill switches and mandatory reporting when AI agents misbehave.

The summit also saw executives from OpenAI, Anthropic, Nvidia, Meta, Google and Elon Musk’s X sign a one-page agreement that Cryptopolitan described as “morally binding.” The signatories pledged to use independent auditors and put safeguards in place to prevent AI models from going rogue.
Microsoft, however, did not sign this accord, according to The Telegraph.
He pointed to its AI Security Institute , launched in 2024 under then prime minister Rishi Sunak as the AI Safety Institute.
The body has secured voluntary agreements allowing it to test frontier models before they ship.
Smith welcomed the agreement and said Microsoft would be willing to sign it.
He called the agreement “a good step” and “a necessary step,” but added that he did not thik it was sufficient any longer.
“Every carton of milk that you see in the grocery store is subject to safety rules and inspection.”

Smith’s “emergency brakes” idea echoes Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella, who called for AI models to carry a mechanism that lets a human pause or shut down a system mid-task if it runs out of control by any chance.

He warned that voluntary commitments may do little to curb the biggest risks, since companies that already take safety seriously are more likely to follow them, while those that pose the greatest danger can choose to ignore them.
